strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and underexplored control point: the initial/BOS token as a target for inference-time attention modulation. The connection to attention sinks is timely and potentially useful.
The proposed mechanism is simple, broadly implementable, and experimentally tested across several model families and attention backends, including eager, SDPA, and Flash-style settings.

The empirical section is fairly broad in task coverage, spanning classification, multiple-choice QA, MT-Bench, few-shot settings, prompt variation, context length, quantization, and decoding strategies.
The paper includes useful diagnostic analyses by token position, layer group, and attention head, which help motivate why uniform global scaling is suboptimal.
weaknesses: The central evaluation protocol is not sufficiently sound. ZeroTuning relies on labeled calibration data and accuracy to classify heads and tune scaling factors, and the paper is unclear about whether the reported benchmark numbers are on held-out test sets distinct from the 500-example validation/calibration set. If selection and reporting use the same samples, many headline gains are likely overfit and not a valid estimate of generalization.

The method is presented as training-free and task-agnostic, but the strongest version is supervised, dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning. This substantially weakens the framing and practical claim, especially since the limitations section acknowledges reliance on ground-truth signals.

Novelty is moderate rather than high. The paper combines known attention-sink observations with inference-time attention scaling; the theoretical analysis is mostly straightforward normalization algebra and does not by itself establish when performance should improve.

Baselines may not be fully fair or optimized. ACT is only run for one model/backend, AutoPASTA details and tuning budget are limited, and comparisons do not clearly equalize access to labeled calibration data or search budget.

The strongest improvements occur on tasks where the base model appears poorly prompted or has many invalid-format outputs, especially SST-2/TREC/SUBJ. This raises concern that the method is partly correcting evaluation-format artifacts rather than improving reasoning or language understanding.

There is little statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, repeated random seeds, significance tests, or sensitivity to calibration-set choice, despite many results being selected through head/gamma search.
The MT-Bench gains are small and judged by GPT-4 without enough detail on variance, prompts, or judge stability, so the evidence for open-ended conversational improvement is weak.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details for head profiling, gamma search ranges, validation/test splits, and exact data subsets are not sufficiently specified for a high-confidence reproduction.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and simple intervention point: the initial/BOS token as a universal attention-scaling target. This is a potentially useful observation and connects naturally to recent work on attention sinks.
The method is lightweight at inference time and is evaluated across several model families and attention implementations, including eager, SDPA, and Flash-style settings.
The paper includes several auxiliary analyses, such as layer/head behavior, robustness to prompt variation, few-shot settings, quantization, decoding strategies, and context length perturbations.
weaknesses: The central framing is misleading: ZeroTuning is described as training-free and task-agnostic, but the full method uses ground-truth validation accuracy, head behavior profiling, and scaling-factor search on 500 labeled examples per dataset. This is supervised per-task calibration, not a universal training-free procedure.

The evaluation appears vulnerable to overfitting and selection bias. The paper does not clearly separate calibration, validation, and test sets, does not report variance or statistical significance, and repeatedly chooses heads/scaling factors based on performance. This substantially weakens the credibility of the reported gains.

The largest improvements occur on classification tasks where the vanilla baselines seem unusually weak, e.g. very low TREC/SUBJ performance for instruction-tuned models. The appendix examples suggest many gains may come from correcting output-format failures rather than improving task understanding, but this is not rigorously analyzed.

Theoretical analysis is mostly elementary algebra about renormalizing one attention weight and does not strongly justify the empirical method. It also abstracts away multi-layer, multi-head, residual, MLP, and generation dynamics, so the claims about sharpening/smoothing and interpretability are much stronger than the theory supports.

The method is much less task-agnostic than claimed: different datasets require different scaling directions, head subsets, and hyperparameters. The paper does not provide a convincing unsupervised rule for choosing these at deployment time; its own limitations section acknowledges this core issue.

Baselines are insufficient and not always comparable. ACT is omitted for SDPA/Flash models, AutoPASTA details are limited, and there are no strong calibration or prompt-format baselines that could test whether the improvements are due simply to better label verbalization or constrained decoding.

Reproducibility is limited. Important implementation details are missing or unclear, including exact train/validation/test splits, sample sizes, hyperparameter search ranges, head-selection criteria, whether test labels influence tuning, and code availability.

The MT-Bench improvements are small and not convincingly supported; the judge setup, randomness, and significance are not reported. These results do not substantiate the broader claim that the method improves multi-turn conversation quality.

The paper contains presentation issues and inconsistencies, such as table typos, duplicated or mislabeled columns, awkward terminology, and occasional mismatch between claims and experimental setup. These reduce confidence in the experimental care.

Overall, the idea is intriguing, but the evidence is not strong enough for a top-tier AI venue. The main claims about universal, training-free, task-agnostic enhancement are not adequately supported, and the evaluation protocol raises serious concerns.

strengths: The paper identifies a simple and intriguing control point: scaling attention to the initial/BOS token. This is a novel and elegant idea relative to prior attention-steering methods that require task-specific token selection.

The empirical coverage is broad, spanning classification, multiple-choice QA, MT-Bench, multiple model families, and different attention implementations including eager, SDPA, and Flash-style settings.
The layer-wise and head-wise analyses are useful and help motivate the final head-specific ZeroTuning procedure rather than presenting it as a black-box heuristic.
Results are consistently positive, with especially large gains on several classification datasets and smaller but steady improvements on multiple-choice QA.
The paper includes several robustness studies, including few-shot settings, prompt variation, decoding strategies, context extension, resource constraints, and quantization.
weaknesses: The method is described as training-free, but the main version uses labeled validation examples to classify heads and search scaling factors. This is a significant qualification: it is better characterized as supervised calibration without parameter updates, and the paper should more clearly separate this from fully unsupervised inference-time tuning.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified. It is unclear whether the 500-sample validation set is always disjoint from test data, how hyperparameter grids are chosen, whether model/dataset-specific choices are tuned on held-out data, and how sensitive results are to validation seed. No error bars or multiple random splits are reported.

Some very large classification gains may partly reflect output-format effects or weak zero-shot prompting rather than deeper task competence. Stronger controls such as constrained decoding, label-token calibration, prompt ensembles, and better verbalizer handling would make the claims more convincing.

The theoretical analysis is intuitive but limited. It mostly formalizes a direct attention-weight rescaling operation and relies on simplifying assumptions; the connection to actual key/query scaling under optimized attention kernels is less clean and can behave abruptly, as the appendix itself shows.

Baselines are somewhat narrow. Comparisons to ACT and AutoPASTA are relevant, but the paper lacks stronger inference-time adaptation and calibration baselines, and ACT is evaluated only for LLaMA eager attention.

The head-selection procedure may overfit dataset-specific validation signals. The paper shows resource-constrained variants, but the strongest reported numbers rely on per-dataset profiling, which limits the strength of claims about universal, task-agnostic tuning.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: exact scaling grids, head-ranking criteria, top-head selection procedure, validation splits, sample sizes per benchmark subset, and implementation details for SDPA/Flash key-state tuning should be made explicit.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and practically attractive inference-time intervention: rescaling attention to the initial/BOS token, avoiding task-specific important-token identification used by prior attention steering methods.
The empirical study is broad, covering multiple model families, attention implementations, task types, robustness settings, quantization, prompt variation, context length, and few-shot scenarios.
The paper includes useful analyses across token positions, layers, heads, and scaling directions, which help motivate why head-specific initial-token tuning can outperform uniform tuning.
The method is lightweight and potentially easy to implement, especially compared with methods requiring explicit attention-map inspection or LLM-based token selection.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol raises significant concerns. The supervised method performs head classification and hyperparameter search on a validation set, but the paper does not clearly establish rigorous separation from test evaluation across all datasets, nor does it quantify overfitting risk from searching many heads and scaling factors.

The unsupervised variant tunes by minimizing entropy on the unlabeled test inputs, which is a transductive test-time selection protocol. This weakens the claim that it requires no calibration data and makes comparison to standard inference baselines less clean.

The theoretical contribution is fairly limited: the main derivation shows how rescaling one attention mass changes pairwise differences among other tokens, but several stronger claims about entropy, pretrained knowledge unlocking, and causal mechanisms are not theoretically established.

Some large gains appear tied to correcting output-format or prompt-following failures rather than deeper task competence, as suggested by the error analyses and very low vanilla scores on some classification datasets. This makes the practical significance of the reported accuracy improvements less clear.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and potentially uneven: ACT is only run on one model, some baseline hyperparameters appear fixed rather than equally searched, and stronger decoding/prompting/calibration baselines are missing.

The paper lacks statistical uncertainty, repeated runs, validation/test split details, and compute/search cost reporting, all of which are important because the method relies on calibration and head selection.

Claims of kernel agnosticism rely on key/query scaling as a surrogate for attention-score scaling, but the paper itself shows this surrogate can be more unstable; this deserves more careful treatment in the main evaluation.

strengths: The paper studies a simple and potentially useful inference-time intervention: scaling attention to the initial/BOS token. The idea is easy to implement and, if validated, would be attractive for deployment because it requires no parameter updates.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad empirical sweep across models, attention implementations, and task families, including classification, multiple-choice QA, MT-Bench, quantization, prompt variants, and context-length tests.

The layer-wise and head-wise analyses are useful exploratory evidence that the initial token can act as a meaningful control point, and the paper makes a plausible connection to the attention-sink literature.
The authors compare against relevant attention-tuning baselines such as ACT and Auto-PASTA, and they include both supervised and unsupervised variants of the method.
The paper is generally readable, and the appendix contains many additional experiments and prompt details.
weaknesses: The main evaluation protocol is not convincing enough for a top-tier venue. Many reported gains, especially the very large SST-2/SUBJ/TREC improvements, appear tied to free-form greedy generation and output-format errors. A much stronger baseline would evaluate classification and multiple-choice tasks by normalized label/choice log-likelihood or constrained decoding. Without this, it is unclear whether ZeroTuning improves reasoning/knowledge or merely changes answer formatting and verbosity.

The supervised variant performs substantial dataset-specific calibration: head profiling, head selection, and scaling-factor search on 500 labeled examples. This is closer to validation-set hyperparameter tuning than purely training-free improvement, and the comparison to vanilla inference and baselines may be unfair unless all methods receive equivalent calibration budgets and search spaces.

The unsupervised variant tunes on the unlabeled test inputs by minimizing average entropy. This is transductive test-set adaptation, not a standard label-free deployment setting, and the paper does not adequately discuss how performance changes when calibration inputs are drawn from a separate distribution or a small held-out unlabeled set.

The theoretical contribution is weak. The monotonicity result largely follows from the algebra of rescaling an existing attention distribution and does not establish that the intervention should improve task performance. Moreover, practical implementations via key/query scaling are not exactly equivalent to multiplying attention weights, especially because scaling keys changes logits exponentially and can interact with logit signs and head geometry.

Claims about “unlocking pretrained knowledge,” “correcting biases,” and interpretability are stronger than the evidence. The paper mostly shows accuracy changes after a perturbation, but does not causally establish the proposed mechanisms beyond suggestive entropy and attention analyses.

The baselines are incomplete. The paper lacks comparisons to simple prompt-format fixes, few-shot formatting baselines for the main tables, constrained answer extraction, calibration/logit-bias methods, temperature/entropy calibration baselines under the same protocol, and other inference-time adaptation methods not based on attention-token selection.

Statistical reliability is underreported. The paper reports many single-number improvements but provides little or no variance across random seeds, validation splits, calibration-set sizes, prompt samples, or MT-Bench judge variability. Some multiple-choice gains are small enough that uncertainty could change the conclusions.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation specifics: exact search grids, head-selection procedure details, evaluation parsing rules, dataset splits/subsampling, generation length limits, and failure handling are not specified sufficiently in the main paper or appendix.

The method may have practical costs and fragility that are underplayed. Head-wise profiling across tasks requires many validation evaluations, and the best direction of scaling differs by dataset. The paper does not sufficiently characterize negative transfer or how a practitioner should choose parameters without task-specific tuning.

Overall, the paper has an interesting observation but the current evidence does not support acceptance. The core results are too entangled with evaluation artifacts and dataset-specific calibration to establish a robust, general-purpose LLM enhancement method.

strengths: The paper proposes a very simple and appealing inference-time intervention: rescaling attention to the initial token rather than identifying task-specific important tokens. This is elegant, easy to implement, and addresses a real limitation of prior attention steering methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad: multiple model families and attention implementations, 15 datasets spanning classification, multiple-choice QA, and MT-Bench, plus comparisons to ACT and Auto-PASTA where applicable.

The results are consistently positive, especially on classification tasks, with large gains for Llama-3.1-8B and meaningful improvements on Qwen and DeepSeek models. The method also appears competitive with stronger token-selection baselines despite using a universal token.

The paper contains useful diagnostic analyses across token positions, layers, heads, context length, few-shot settings, decoding strategies, prompt variations, quantization, and resource constraints. These analyses make the contribution more convincing than a single benchmark table would.

The supervised and entropy-based unsupervised variants are practically interesting, and the discussion of failure modes and extreme scaling behavior is a welcome attempt to define the method's limits.
weaknesses: The central theoretical analysis is somewhat overclaimed. It shows how rescaling the initial token changes relative attention differences among other tokens, but it does not theoretically justify improvements in task accuracy, output entropy, factuality, or reasoning quality. Claims about unlocking pretrained knowledge and monotonic control of entropy are mostly empirical and should be stated more carefully.

The calibration protocol needs clearer safeguards against overfitting. The method profiles heads and searches scaling factors on 500 validation examples, but the paper does not sufficiently detail dataset splits, test sample sizes, hyperparameter grids, or whether choices were tuned per dataset/model after observing results. This is important because the gains can be highly sensitive to gamma and head subsets.

The unsupervised variant minimizes entropy on the unlabeled test inputs, which is a transductive setting. This may be acceptable in some deployments, but it is not the same as generally label-free deployment, and the paper should evaluate transfer of entropy-chosen parameters from calibration inputs to held-out inputs.

The comparison set is reasonable but incomplete. There are no comparisons to broader inference-time adaptation/calibration methods beyond ACT and Auto-PASTA, and ACT is omitted for SDPA/Flash models due implementation constraints. This makes it harder to judge whether the gains come from the initial-token insight specifically or from task-level hyperparameter calibration.

Some reported gains, especially on classification datasets such as SST-2 and SUBJ, are unusually large and may partly reflect improved answer-format compliance rather than semantic improvement. The paper discusses this qualitatively, but should report invalid-output rates and constrained decoding or exact-choice scoring baselines.

The computational cost of head profiling and parameter search is under-specified. The method is advertised as lightweight and four lines of code, but full supervised ZeroTuning may require many calibration forward passes over heads and gamma values; wall-clock and memory overhead should be reported.

The paper would benefit from statistical uncertainty over random validation selections, prompt variants, and benchmark subsamples. Most results are single-number reports without confidence intervals or multiple seeds, which weakens evidence for smaller gains on multiple-choice and MT-Bench.
